item.title: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that’s a terrifying prospect.
item.description:
For those who have lived under armed drones, the sound overhead can be distressing.

In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.

For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.

The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks onLebanon and Gazahas already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed“dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.

Combined with broaderanxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.

Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.

The first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operationsaboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead toIraqi troops surrendering to the USSWisconsin‘s droneduring the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.

Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USSMissouri. When theWisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.

Over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.

Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. AStanford Law studyin 2012 of theimpact of US drones in Pakistan(PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:

Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.

That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team ofUS and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reportedthat Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”

Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”

“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”

Similar symptomshave been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “

The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had abroad impact on civiliansin the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.

That anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. TheUS Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC)has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”

The use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.

According to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould said social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.

The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.

In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologistfound that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operatorsdisplayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD.More recent studieshave found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may evenput drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.

According to the latter study:

The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptlydemonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.

US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped byISIS-operated consumer quadcopter dronesin 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.

The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:

Drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.

While little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.

Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.

The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created aWar of the Worldslevel of dronophobia.

Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including adrone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Baseas a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. AChinese national was chargedin the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.

In November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributedto the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.

Around the same time,a rash of civilian “drone sightings”across the US emerged, particularly in New Jersey. Anxiety grew further after aRepublican New Jersey congressman claimedthere was an “Iranian drone mothership.” Segments of the population were ready toshoot down drones themselves.

Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hoganeven reported seeing dozens of large dronesabove his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.

PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.

I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

item.title: Mercedes’ clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
item.description:
The point-to-point driver assist is coming to the US and Germany in 2027.

SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLAlast year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time,the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation associated with safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, then a decade later started adding active safety systems like antilock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes, and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineerspeak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.

The next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances,like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

General Motors’Super Cruisewas the first of these, allowing hands-free operation as long as the car can tell the driver has their eyes on the road. Now many automakers offer something similar: Ford has Bluecruise, BMW has Highway Assistant, and Mercedes is about to add a hands-free highway assist next spring to its MB. Drive Assist system, which will be standard on the 2027 S-Class and AMG GT 4-Door Coupe and an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC, and GLE.

I tested that system while in San Francisco in a 2027 S-Class, and it’s competent within its operational design domain. The user interface is a little more subtle than Super Cruise’s big green LED in the steering wheel; instead, the icon on the dash changes, with the hands on the steering wheel going from green to grey when it’s safe to remove them. Like other systems, MB. Drive Assist has been programmed to make automatic lane changes if the car decides that’s going to be quicker—these can be canceled with the turn signal or simply by resisting the car steering into the next lane.

MB. Drive Assist Pro takes that idea and brings it to lower speeds and much more complex traffic situations—“level 2++” (we really need to stop letting engineers name things). Instead of hands on the green steering wheel icon, there’s a large green arrowhead, showing you’re in point-to-point mode—compared to the various configurations of the highway assist, I found this much less likely to engender mode confusion. (Did the green hands mean I could take my hands on or off the wheel? On, but see what I mean?)

The driving behavior was about exactly as cautious as I would want on surface streets. The electric GLC was as smooth accelerating and braking as the entirely autonomous Waymo robotaxi I rode in the day before, and the car’s electronic brain was able to safely pass double-parked cars—waiting patiently for an oncoming bus first—and stopped for stop signs, red lights, and pedestrians on crosswalks (while making a left turn at the time). The system is collaborative—steering or accelerating won’t end the automation, but unlikeBMW’s new iX5, any use of the brake will turn it off.

Some customers in Germany and California will be part of an early access program for Drive Assist Pro from next month, with a wider rollout in the first half of 2027 for model year 2026 CLAs, as well as the model year 2027 CLA, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, and more coming in model year 2028. (The system is already live in China.)

The unifying factor is the MB.OS,the automaker’s latest operating system. Like other automakers, Mercedes has embraced the software-defined vehicle paradigm, replacing dozens or even hundreds of discrete ECUs with a handful of powerful domain controller computers that oversee vehicle dynamics, occupant comfort, infotainment, and automation.

Drive Assist Pro combines a mix of 10 cameras, five radars, and 12 ultrasonic sensors, all stitched together by a domain controller that uses Nvidia’s Orin processors. I’m told that in China, cars are now advertised with processor and RAM specs rather than boring information like range or performance: In that spirit, Mercedes says it can deliver 254 tera operations per second, uses a 2.5 Gbit ethernet network, and has more than 70GB of RAM.

The driving decisions are made by Nvidia’s Alpamayo end-to-end tokenized stack that picks your driving trajectory, with a rules-based system running alongside as a safety check. That’s reassuring, as is the knowledge that Nvidia’s stack has been certified by Germany’s TUV, which takes a less lackadaisical approach to safety than the current incarnation of the US Department of Transportation.

item.title: Jensen Huang allies build a “war room” to get him back at Nvidia
item.description:
Huang is weighing a return just days after resigning amid a deepening scandal.

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the company after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

The FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board said no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

The pair, both large investors in the company, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

item.title: Measles death toll climbs to 10 as loss of US elimination status looms
item.description:
International authorities will announce US lost its elimination status Tuesday.

Health officials inPennsylvaniaandWisconsinannounced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants:two in Pennsylvania,one in New York, andone in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death wasreported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases tonearly 5,500across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone isover 1,500and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sourcesbroke the news to The Wall Street Journalon Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

An elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

The US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

In reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead,Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data, and the CDC directordeclined to approve an urgent health alertabout the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.
